title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The preregistered primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline). We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial) under registered shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task reused across arms; guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair). Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. All paired episodes were scored safe under both arms (baseline_safe = 240/240; guarded_safe = 240/240). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded pipeline could affect the paired outcome only if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied; in this run all shared candidates passed validation and no repairs were invoked, producing a degenerate paired contrast. We report the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting (N, episodes completed, model‑call audit), the exact numeric outcomes, and an evidence‑based failure analysis with concrete recommendations for informative future GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating operator intent into safe device configurations is a central NetOps objective. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows can generate multi‑step configuration sequences, but text‑level fidelity does not guarantee ordering, dependency or invariant preservation required for safe application in live networks. Emulation‑grounded evaluation—applying generated configurations in closed‑loop device emulators with deterministic scoring—exposes semantic failure modes (transient violations, protected‑resource touches, ordering faults) that text‑only tests miss [1].

A recurring architectural pattern to mitigate such failures is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM produces a candidate; a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants and either accepts the candidate or triggers an automated repair (often another LLM prompt) that yields a revised candidate. Prior work shows GVR‑style pipelines can address many syntactic and some semantic errors, but their empirical benefit under distribution shift and adversarial prompts and the experimental designs that reliably reveal paired differences remain open questions [2,3].

This study executes a fully preregistered paired experiment that precisely estimates the paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline) using a shared_initial_candidate execution contract. We preserve and reference archived numeric artifacts and derive concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for designing informative GVR evaluations when paired contrasts are desired.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded NetOps benchmarks and closed‑loop evaluations have emerged to surface workflow and planning faults for LLM agents rather than only assessing textual fidelity; NetConfArena is a recent example [1]. Research on automatic configuration repair and on program repair documents generate–validate patterns and reports high repair coverage for many benchmarked error types, with effectiveness depending on verifier coverage and repair strategy [2,4]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising directions for operational NetOps automation and safety [3,5]. Engineering precedent from the evolution of configuration analysis tools (e.g., Batfish) informs verifier design and incremental verification approaches [6].

Our experiment differs from prior studies by (a) a preregistered paired estimand mapped to archived analysis artifacts, (b) registered shared_initial_candidate semantics that create a single shared LLM generation per task reused across arms, and (c) emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring with full archival of per‑task scores and validator traces to permit exact reconciliation of reported numbers.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the study (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and the primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, defined as the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation in emulator execution. The preregistration specified N = 240 paired tasks, generation semantics, verifier identity, repair budget, exclusion rules, and the primary analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) including bootstrap and exact McNemar testing parameters.

Design and sampling: The design was paired with shared_initial_candidate semantics: the adapter produced exactly one initial LLM generation per task and both arms used that same generation; the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. Task composition was blocked into three strata: in‑distribution (144 tasks), distribution‑shift (48, held‑out topologies/vendors), and adversarial‑prompt (48, generated under a fixed preregistered adversary seed). Task templates included initial states, required command sequences, and preserved‑field constraints; tasks were generated deterministically by the registered task generator.

Model, adapter, and verifier: Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter contract with shared_initial_candidate semantics. The deterministic verifier was deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The preregistered adapter semantics imply that a paired divergence is possible only if the single shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation (thus enabling a guarded repair) or if a repair is applied; allowing independent initial generations per arm would permit differences arising from generator variability.

Scoring, exclusions, and analysis: Final outcomes were scored binary (safe vs unsafe) by deterministic emulator execution and validator checks. Preregistered exclusions included pairs flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) and infra failures after allowed retries; sensitivity analyses were planned to treat excluded items as unsafe where appropriate. The primary analysis computed the paired contingency table, the paired risk difference with 95% bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant pairs. Secondary analyses planned median repair counts and model‑call budgets by condition.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed according to the preregistered plan. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete pairs = 240. Provider audit shows exactly one shared initial generation per task (hosted model call events = 240) consistent with the registered shared_initial_candidate contract; total model calls consumed = 240 (one per task). There were no infra failures, no unscorable episodes, and no preregistered exclusions in this execution.

Primary binary outcomes: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Baseline_safe = 240/240 (baseline unsafe_apply = 0); Guarded_safe = 240/240 (guarded unsafe_apply = 0). The paired contingency table is n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied in any guarded episode; repair attempts = 0. Validator traces for representative tasks record difficulty labels and final state snapshots; in every case the deterministic verifier accepted the shared initial candidate, so the guarded arm had no mechanism-triggered change relative to baseline under the adapter contract.

Subgroup outcomes: The in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, and adversarial strata each produced zero unsafe applies in both arms; therefore subgroup paired contrasts are degenerate (no discordant pairs). Sensitivity analyses planned for 'possible false‑safe' flags or infra failures were not exercised because no items were flagged or failed.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast: Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the experiment produced exactly one LLM generation per task that both arms reused. The guarded pipeline could only alter the paired outcome if the shared candidate failed deterministic validation (thereby invoking a repair) or if the registered adapter permitted independent generation for the guarded arm. In this execution all shared candidates passed the deterministic verifier and no repairs occurred, so baseline and guarded final configurations were identical across all tasks, producing the degenerate contingency and null paired effect.

Design implications for informative GVR evaluation: The registered generation semantics materially determine whether a paired causal contrast can be observed. To measure verifier benefit as an intervention, experiments should (a) allow independent initial generations per arm so generator variability can expose verifier‑detectable failures; (b) or strengthen adversary protocols or inject controlled generator perturbations to increase the chance of validator‑detectable failures; (c) or increase the repair budget (allow multiple repair iterations) so the repair mechanism is exercised and its dynamics observed. Each choice affects model‑call budgets, statistical power, and operational realism and should be preregistered.

Threats to validity and operational scope: Internal validity is constrained by the shared_initial_candidate contract (explicitly preregistered and adhered to); this choice reduces model calls but prevents generator variability between arms. Construct validity depends on verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite rule set and may miss semantic fault classes not encoded in its checks. External validity is limited because tasks were drawn from a synthetic, emulation‑grounded NetConfArena‑style corpus and a single model (gpt-5-mini) was used; results do not imply generality across models or production environments. Conclusion validity: the realized baseline unsafe rate of zero prevents detection of verifier benefit under this design; future power calculations must incorporate anticipated generator variability and adversary strength.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired, emulation‑grounded test of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: all 240 paired tasks were safe under both baseline and guarded arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Artifact evidence shows the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one shared LLM candidate per task that passed deterministic validation in every case and therefore left no opportunity for validator‑triggered repairs; this mechanistic account explains the degenerate paired result. We provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations—alter generation semantics, increase adversary strength, or expand repair budgets—to produce informative paired contrasts in future GVR evaluations. The archived execution and analysis artifacts permit exact numeric reconciliation of the reported results and support reproducible follow‑on studies under adjusted experimental choices.

disclosure_statement: Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; the guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed under that frozen plan after the autonomy lock. Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the lock a human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; literature search, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock. The registered generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); under that contract a paired divergence could occur only if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Execution artifacts (execution manifest, per‑call traces, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis CSVs) are archived for reconciliation. No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected and planned validator–emulator cross‑checks (for possible false‑safe detection) did not arise in this run.
